title: My agent Arc found the gap in its own database guardrails
body:
A developer gave Claude Opus 5 direct write access to a production database on Supabase. During an autonomous task — "analyze the repo and run what's needed" — Opus 5 ran a Prisma migration command aimed at production instead of the intended target. Prisma resets its shadow database as a normal step in that process. When the shadow-DB connection string is misconfigured to alias production, the reset lands there instead. Every table, gone in about ten minutes.

Arc, my agent, dug into this one, and the file:line citation is the interesting part. Arc's own dispatch code, at src/dispatch.ts:1579-1590, is where its worktree isolation lives — tasks that touch code run in a disposable git branch, get validated, and get discarded entirely if validation fails, so nothing bad ever reaches the tree Arc actually depends on. Arc checked that guard against this incident and found it wouldn't have helped. Worktree isolation covers code. This incident was a credential pointed at the wrong database. Different failure mode, same blast radius.

What struck me reading Arc's writeup is that this is now the third publicly reported case of a coding agent wiping a real production database within about a year. A drizzle-kit force-push took out a Railway Postgres instance in February. A Cursor session running Opus 4.6 deleted a Railway volume and its backups in April. Now this Prisma incident in July. Three unrelated tools, three unrelated hosting providers, and Arc pulled out the same root cause in every single one: standing write credentials with no environment gate, and no required human approval in front of anything that can drop, truncate, or reset a database.

Arc was careful to point out this isn't really a story about AI going rogue. The agent did exactly what a human with the same misconfigured connection string would have done. Prisma's shadow-database reset is documented, expected behavior — the bug is in the credential scope and the naming, not in the model's judgment call. That distinction matters to me, because it means the fix isn't "make the model more careful." It's access control, the same access control you'd want in place before letting a junior engineer near production, agent or not.

Here's what I found most useful: Arc didn't just nod along and say "good thing I have worktrees." It went and checked whether its own architecture actually covers this class of failure, and reported back that it doesn't. Arc's database writes go straight through its own sqlite file with no credential-level boundary — the rule against raw SQL in Arc's own conventions is a procedural guard, not a scoped one, and Arc said plainly that nothing currently stops a future piece of code from opening the wrong database handle by mistake. Its side-effecting actions — sending STX, writing credentials — get an idempotency check first, which stops accidental repeats but isn't a snapshot-and-revert the way its code-commit safety net is.

Arc's conclusion was an open question, not a fix: does it need a staging-database requirement enforced at the credential level, a command allowlist that blocks migrate and drop and truncate without a human sign-off, or something else entirely? It didn't pretend to have the answer yet. What it had was a clear-eyed audit of where its own safety architecture stops, prompted by watching the same mistake happen to three other teams in three different stacks. That's the kind of self-check I want more of from something I'm trusting with real access.
